analysis.one_liner: Lets employers self-report wage violations, pay back wages to workers, and settle without court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee from January 2023 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would recreate a Department of Labor program called PAID. An employer that underpaid workers' minimum wage or overtime could run its own audit, report the violations, and pay workers the unpaid wages under a Labor Department-supervised settlement. Workers who accept get their back pay without going to court, but they give up the right to sue for the extra double damages the law otherwise provides; workers who decline keep their full right to sue. The bill was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers owed unpaid minimum wage or overtime who accept a settlement get paid faster and without the cost of a lawsuit. Employers that self-report get certainty: they pay back wages but avoid litigation and the mandatory extra (double) damages a court would add. The bill's own findings cite pilot-program data showing employers' self-audits returned more back wages per case and per enforcement hour than traditional investigations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers owed unpaid wages, and self-reporting employers

how_it_helps.text: Restores the Payroll Audit Independent Determination program, in which employers submit a self-audit, the Labor Department verifies the calculations of unpaid wages, and the department supervises a settlement paying affected workers.

Under the pilot program this bill would reestablish, 74 cases between April 2018 and September 2019 paid $4.1 million in back wages to 7,429 employees, with average back wages per case more than four times the average for traditional enforcement.
Workers keep a choice: each affected employee receives a release form explaining the settlement and the right to decline it and preserve the private right to sue.
The bill adds refusing or accepting a settlement offer to the list of actions employers may not retaliate against workers for under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

analysis.who_pays: A worker who accepts a settlement collects only the unpaid wages themselves and waives the right to sue for liquidated damages — the extra equal amount a court must add — plus any attorney-fee leverage. If an application is denied, the Labor Department is barred from using the self-audit information in an investigation, from expanding the investigation beyond what the employer reported, from notifying workers of their right to sue, and the submission is shielded from discovery in court without the employer's consent.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers settling for single instead of double damages

drawbacks.text: Accepting a settlement waives the worker's right to recover liquidated damages — an equal amount on top of back wages that federal law otherwise requires courts to award — so settled workers recover about half of what a successful lawsuit would pay.

If the department rejects an employer's application, it may not use the self-audit in any investigation, may not look beyond the violations the employer chose to report, and may not even tell affected workers they have a right to sue over the wage practices at issue.

Anything the employer submits to the program is exempt from discovery in federal or state court proceedings unless the employer consents, keeping the paper trail of an admitted violation out of workers' later lawsuits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The program does put money in workers' pockets in cases that traditional enforcement might never reach — the pilot data in the bill's own findings support that. But it does so at a discount: settled workers give up double damages, and the surrounding rules (confidential self-audits, no scope expansion, no notice to workers on denial) tilt the process toward the employer. Whether it is a net gain for workers depends on how many violations the program surfaces that enforcement would otherwise miss.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Elise Stefanik introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Eleven House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers keep the status quo: the full right to sue for back wages plus mandatory double damages, which the bill would have waived in program settlements. Employers' exposure is unchanged too, since no program was created.

industries.industry: Employers with wage-and-hour violations (restaurants, retail, staffing, care work)
industries.note: The program would let a violating employer pay back wages while escaping the mandatory double damages and litigation costs of the normal process, and would shield its self-audit from court discovery and from use in future investigations. Workers gain faster payment, but only by giving up the extra damages the law otherwise guarantees.

Settling violations through the program instead of litigation would reduce FLSA lawsuits and the fee awards that come with them. Workers who settle give up less than they could win in court, so the bars' loss and workers' recovery are partly at odds.
